name: The Life You Can Save (charityevals' estimate)
summary: The Life You Can Save recommends about thirty global health and poverty charities and gets people to give to them, through its own giving channels in the US and Australia and by influencing gifts made to the charities directly. In 2025 it moved $24.1 million by its own report (about $25 million once gifts nobody reported are allowed for) for $2.6 million of operating costs, about $9.3 moved per dollar of cost after Founders Pledge's share of the fund they ran together, of which 91% is credited to it after the donated services it received; each dollar moved is valued where its money went (its own split by charity, each charity at its live result on this site), half of it as new money and the rest only for the gain over GiveDirectly, and the next dollar at the shared share of the past average. It comes out more than ten times its peers because each of its dollars moves about nine dollars to charities that are themselves among the site's better global-health results: its result is a multiple of theirs, not a separate intervention. Nearly all the uncertainty is in shared judgments (how much the next dollar does compared with the average, how much of the money donors would have given anyway), and 15 of its 34 destinations (44% of the money, none modelled here) are valued at the average of the rest.

rows.label: Operating expenses on the programme (all of them)
rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save has one programme: recommending charities (research and evaluation) and getting people to give to them (outreach, the book, workplace and online giving, donor services, the Australian and UK giving channels). Its management and its fundraising serve that programme, which is itself fundraising for other charities, so all operating expenses are programme cost and the overhead multiplier is 1. The Form 990's split (most of the US cost under fundraising) doesn't change the total cost of the money moved.

rows.label: Spending on the modelled programme in 2025 (raising money for its recommended charities)
rows.explainer: The whole operating budget of both entities in calendar 2025, the latest year with both a filed Form 990 and a published money-moved report. No part of the work is left out: every activity aims at the money moved. The Life You Can Save says both entities are independently audited; the 2025 audited statements themselves are not posted, so the 990 (filed October 2026) and the charity's 2025 financials summary are the sources.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Influenced gifts actually made, per dollar reported (charities', donors' and intermediaries' reports)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The three reported channels count only gifts someone told the charity about: by its own account only about half its recommended charities report any, fewer than 100 donors reported theirs, and some giving platforms have no tracking. If the non-reporting charities received half as much influenced money per charity as the reporting ones, the true total would be about 1.5 times the reported one; we take 1.25 because the charities that report are likely the ones with the most such gifts. Low 0.9: only what was reported, less some overlap, since the source doesn't say a gift reported by both the charity and the donor is counted once. High 2: as much again unreported. This is about counting the gifts, not whether they were caused by the charity: that is the shared new-money share's question.

source.title: The Life You Can Save, Money Moved 2025: By Charity

rows.explainer: The emergency fund it ran with Founders Pledge after the 2025 aid cuts ($13.1 million in all, by its annual report); this is the part it counts as its own money moved.

rows.label: Its share of the credit for the Rapid Response Fund money it counts
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The fund was a joint campaign with Founders Pledge (and Project Resource Optimization), whose own outreach and grant-making stand behind the same gifts (Convention 2: credit is the charity's share of the resources behind the outcome). The $3.1 million it counts is the part given through its own channels, so it keeps most of the credit: 75%, from an even split with Founders Pledge (50%) to all of it (100%). Only this co-run fund is shared; the other channels are its own outreach.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for its recommended charities in 2025, credited to it (US$)
rows.explainer: Gross money moved less the part of the Rapid Response Fund credited to Founders Pledge. Valued only through the shared rows below: whether donors would have given anyway is the site's one new-money share, where the money goes is the charity's own published split, and the next dollar against this year's average is the shared slider. No leverage ratio or counterfactual share of the charity's own is used.

rows.label: Value per unit affected per year, in units of value
rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save does no policy or research work whose value runs outside the money it moves (its charity research serves the recommendations that move money, and is valued through it), so this branch is 0. Its value per unit is 0 too, so the branch adds nothing.

rows.label: Probability the change happens because of this work
rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save does no policy or research work whose value runs outside the money it moves (its charity research serves the recommendations that move money, and is valued through it), so this branch is 0. No chance of success is needed: The Life You Can Save has moved money for over a decade, so it isn't a not-yet-proven organisation and takes no success step.

Value of a dollar to The Life You Can Save's recommended charities (its 2025 split, live), units of value
rows.explainer: The Life You Can Save's own published split of the money it moved in 2025, by charity, each charity at its main model's live result on this site (GiveDirectly at GiveWell's model, as everywhere in meta models); Evidence Action and Malaria Consortium, which run several programmes, at GiveWell's programme-weighted figure for the charity, as on the rankings (Evidence Action: syphilis screening, iron and folic acid, deworming, in-line chlorination and Dispensers for Safe Water; Malaria Consortium: seasonal malaria chemoprevention over its locations, bed nets and vitamin A). The 19 charities with a model here took $13.4 million of the $24.1 million; the rest (14 charities and its Rapid Response Fund, none modelled here) is valued at the average of these, so it drops out of the mix.

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.explainer: Others' resources behind the same money moved: the audited statements count $250,000 of donated services (total expenses per audited statements $2,436,517 against $2,186,517 on the 990). By Convention 2 it stays out of the cost and lowers the charity's share of credit instead. The Australian entity publishes no in-kind figure.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Applies only to the policy and research branch, which is 0 here, so it is 1. Money moved takes its counterfactual through the shared new-money share, and its credit through the Rapid Response Fund share and the attribution share below; nothing else is adjusted, by the site's one method.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Applies only to the policy and research branch, which is 0 here, so it is 1. Money moved takes its counterfactual through the shared new-money share, and its credit through the Rapid Response Fund share and the attribution share below; nothing else is adjusted, by the site's one method.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the money moved: its own operating cost against that cost plus the donated services it received (Convention 2), 91%. The Rapid Response Fund's co-run credit is taken in the reach section. Applied to the money moved as well as to the (zero) policy branch.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Total value (units of value)
rows.explainer: The value of the money moved, times the charity's share of the resources behind it (the donated services); the policy and career branches are 0. The other adjustments stay with the policy branch, so nothing is counted twice.

rows.label: Value per dollar
rows.explainer: For WELLBYs, rename the uov_* rows to wellbys_* and report in wellby. For animals, rename them to sads_* and add the species section of the corporate-campaign template (output ced_per_donor_dollar). For climate, start from the climate skeleton.
